Reading the plotted lines (approximate, derived from page data): TrueType, fontdue about 15 us vs FreeType 2 about 45 us at 10 px/em (about 3x) and about 235 us vs about 545 us at 200 px/em (about 2.3x); OpenType/CFF, fontdue about 12 us vs FreeType about 135 us at 10 px/em (about 11x) and about 220 us vs about 625 us at 200 px/em (about 2.8x). Layout plot: fontdue about 24 us vs glyph_brush_layout about 139 us at 1000 characters (about 5.8x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Rust, no_std, pure-Rust rasterizer and naive layout only; no text shaping (author points to Cosmic Text for that), no hinting. Fonts are fully parsed into custom structures on load (slow, allocating load is an explicit non-goal to fix), so it wins on per-glyph latency, not load time. Not directly usable from C++ without writing an FFI layer.
caveats: Evidence is plots in /images (rasterize_glyf.png, rasterize_cff.png, layout.png) with no table, CPU model, compiler or flags. Benchmark code is public (dev/benches/rasterize.rs and layout.rs, criterion, FreeType benchmark behind the freetype_benchmark feature, freetype-rs 0.26). The FreeType side calls load_char with LoadFlag::RENDER only, so FreeType runs with its default hinting on while fontdue does not hint, and set_char_size is called inside the timed loop; this is not an apples-to-apples comparison. Numbers above are eyeballed from the chart images. fontdue began as a fork of font-rs and was rewritten; font-rs itself is a separate entry.

workload: OpenType shaping of word, sentence and paragraph texts in Latin, Arabic, Hebrew, Hindi, Thai, Khmer, Myanmar and CJK with Noto fonts, plus glyph path extraction and text to SVG, run under Bun with a batch timer (bench/shaping.test.ts).

No hardware, Bun version or runtime flags are stated. Only 3 timed iterations per benchmark in the harness. name: uni-algo
baseline: ICU (word break and extended grapheme cluster break iteration over UTF-16 text)
workload: Unicode text segmentation (UAX #29 word breaks and extended grapheme cluster breaks) over a 'real text' sample in UTF-16, five consecutive runs per configuration.
claimed_speedup: MSVC 19.12 x64, first run: word breaks 2355.47 (uni-algo) vs 11379.4 (ICU), ~4.8x; grapheme breaks 2067.16 vs 5600.95, ~2.7x. MSVC 19.12 x86: word breaks 2544.55 vs 13137.1, ~5.2x; grapheme breaks 2239.48 vs 6766.44, ~3.0x (ratios derived from page data; units are not stated, lower is assumed better).

caveats: Category fit is weak: the benchmarked task is Unicode segmentation, a pre-step of text layout, not font shaping or rasterization, and the baseline is ICU rather than HarfBuzz or FreeType. Results use 2018-era toolchains (GCC 7.3, MSVC 2017), and the perf commits date from April 2023. The result file states no units, no CPU model, no ICU version and no description of the text sample; ICU was measured only under MSVC. The author calls his own perf test 'a mess', and the README claims only performance 'at least the same as other implementations'. Only the UTF-16 segmentation test exists because ICU cluster breaks do not support UTF-8.

name: fpng
workload: Encode and decode 24/32-bit PNG images; in the cited QOIR run, the QOI benchmark suite images, single-threaded, megapixels per second.
claimed_speedup: Independent run in doc/full_benchmarks.txt: PNG/fpng 192.16 EncMPixels/s and 148.19 DecMPixels/s vs PNG/libpng 5.49 and 56.18 (about 35x encode and 2.6x decode, derived from page data); compression ratio 0.3115 vs libpng 0.2423 (lower is better). fpng's own README separately claims 'about 23x faster compression, 2.5-3x faster decompression' than libpng.
compiler_and_flags: gcc (Debian 10.2.1-6) 10.2.1; script/run_full_benchmarks.sh defaults to CFLAGS '-Wall -O3' and compiles the codec adapters with -march=native; libpng and libwebp are Debian Bullseye system builds (their build flags are not stated); fpng's own README benchmarks used MSVC 2019 (flags not stated)
hardware: Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-10210U CPU @ 1.60GHz (desktop/laptop, single-threaded), Debian Bullseye; fpng README numbers were taken on a Xeon E5-2690 3.00 GHz
tradeoffs: The fast decoder only decodes PNG files written by fpng (it checks a private fdEC chunk and returns FPNG_DECODE_NOT_FPNG otherwise), so for arbitrary PNGs a general decoder such as libpng or Wuffs is still needed. Encoder uses only filter 2 and RLE-style matches of distance 3 or 4 with precomputed Huffman tables, so files are much larger than libpng (about 29% larger in the cited run). 24/32bpp only, SSE4.1+PCLMUL for the speed-ups, SIMD only on x86; public domain (Unlicense), so no patent grant.
caveats: The README's own table does not include libpng: its libpng claim is a prose line and its decode speed-up is measured on fpng-compressed PNGs only. The A tier comes from nigeltao/qoir's public benchmark script (one i5-10210U, gcc 10.2.1, Debian libpng). The decoder is limited to fpng's own output, which flatters decode numbers; the author recommends Wuffs for reading arbitrary PNGs.
found_via: WebSearch 'fast PNG decoder encoder faster than libpng SIMD library site:github.com' (result richgel999/fpng); opened README and cross-checked against nigeltao/qoir doc/full_benchmarks.txt

baseline: libpng (Debian Bullseye build); also libwebp lossless (Debian Bullseye build) and libjxl lossless
workload: Lossless encode and decode of the QOI benchmark suite images (qoiformat.org benchmark tarball), single-threaded, megapixels per second plus compression ratio.
claimed_speedup: doc/full_benchmarks.txt: QOIR_Lossless 168.90 EncMPixels/s and 276.45 DecMPixels/s vs PNG/libpng 5.49 and 56.18 (about 31x encode and 4.9x decode, derived from page data; the README states 30x and 4.9x) and vs WebP_Lossless 2.49 and 89.94 (about 68x encode and 3.1x decode, derived from page data). Compression ratio 0.2525 vs libpng 0.2423 and WebP_Lossless 0.1651 (lower is better).
compiler_and_flags: gcc (Debian 10.2.1-6) 10.2.1; script/run_full_benchmarks.sh defaults to CFLAGS '-Wall -O3' and compiles the codec adapters with -march=native; libpng and libwebp are Debian Bullseye system builds (their build flags are not stated)

Compresses worse than libpng and much worse than WebP lossless (0.2525 vs 0.2423 and 0.1651). Single-file C library (src/qoir.h), no dependencies, bundles its own LZ4; tiles allow multi-threaded decode. Lossless 24-bit RGB or 32-bit RGBA only, plus a trivial lossy mode.
caveats: Author's own benchmark, but the full script, adapters and raw output are public. Baselines are Debian system libpng and libwebp, so their compiler flags are unstated; one laptop-class CPU (i5-10210U) and gcc 10.2.1. In the same table Wuffs' PNG decoder decodes at 140.79 MPixels/s (vs libpng 56.18), and the README says ZPNG is 'very competitive with and sometimes strictly better than QOIR'. AVIF was not measured (author hit Debian bug 976349), so there is no libavif comparison. An independent suite (WangXuan95/Image-Compression-Benchmark, CLIC2021) also lists QOIR at 23.696 compress and 19.752 decompress vs Pillow PNG 334.791 and 33.677 (unit not stated on that page).

name: CharLS
baseline: Pillow PNG encoder and Pillow JPEG 2000 plugin (in Image-Compression-Benchmark); the README compares against the original HP JPEG-LS code, JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000
workload: Lossless compression and decompression of 585 CLIC2021 RGB 24-bit images (4.1 GB), single-threaded, total time and total size, using the CharLS-based pillow-jpls 1.3.2 plugin.
claimed_speedup: Image-Compression-Benchmark (CLIC2021, units not stated on page, presumably seconds): JPEG-LS compress 72.237 and decompress 66.567 vs JPEG2000 319.912 and 275.398 (about 4.4x and 4.1x faster, derived from page data) and vs PNG (optimize=False) 334.791 and 33.677 (4.6x faster compress but about 2x slower decompress); JPEG-LS total size 1931584595 vs JPEG2000 1992860964 and PNG 2003016524 bytes. CharLS README: 'about twice as fast as the original HP code, and beats both JPEG-XR and JPEG 2000 by a factor 3'.
compiler_and_flags: Python 3.9 with Pillow 10.1.0 and pillow-jpls 1.3.2 (CharLS wheel build flags not stated)
hardware: Intel Core i7 12700H, 16GB DDR4-3200, Windows 10
tradeoffs: JPEG-LS (ISO/IEC 14495-1) is a lossless/near-lossless codec with low complexity; decode is about twice as slow as Pillow's PNG decode in the cited suite. README notes Hewlett Packard patents on JPEG-LS (licensed free for conformant implementations; some may have expired). No SIMD: speed comes from templates and traits.

The suite measures a Python wrapper (pillow-jpls, which PyPI says is based on CharLS), so Python overhead is included. The README's own 'twice as fast as HP code' claim cites a page on imagecompression.info that was not opened and is dated. Another JPEG-LS-family row ('JPEG-LS-ext') is a different codec and is not counted here.

name: libspng
workload: PNG decode of six images (19k 8bpp, 40k 24bpp, 77k 8bpp, 552k 32bpp, 4002k 24bpp) in the Wuffs benchmark harness, MB/s of decoded output.
claimed_speedup: Wuffs blog appendix (third-party measurement): libspng decodes 1.02x to 1.62x faster than libpng, for example libspng_decode_552k_32bpp_ignore_checksum/clang9 236MB/s vs libpng 146MB/s (1.62x) and libspng_decode_40k_24bpp/gcc10 77.5MB/s vs libpng 73.1MB/s (1.06x). The libspng README claims it 'outperforms the reference implementation in common use cases' with a chart image only.
compiler_and_flags: clang 9 and gcc 10 (flags not stated in the appendix)
tradeoffs: C library with an API incompatible with libpng. Feature gaps: animated PNG only planned; gamma correction not implemented for some output formats and some G8/GA8/GA16 conversions are not supported. Code is BSD-2-Clause but contains libpng-derived optimizations and test images under the PNG Reference Library License v2. Can build against miniz instead of zlib.
caveats: Numbers come from the Wuffs author's blog (the Wuffs harness code is public, but the post does not state the CPU model, so tier B rather than A) against Debian's system libpng; the gain is modest and image-dependent (1.02x on small 8bpp images). The same blog shows libpng with zlib-ng is 1.01x to 1.21x faster than stock libpng, which narrows the gap. mango's README (t0rakka/mango, i7-11800H, 2560x1600) lists spng at 37.7 ms decode and 215.9 ms encode vs libpng 57.3 ms and 820.5 ms, consistent with a 1.5x decode and 3.8x encode gain (derived from page data).
found_via: WebSearch 'lossless image codec faster than libwebp lossless PNG encoder decoder C++ github benchmark' surfaced the Wuffs blog; its appendix lists libspng; confirmed with the libspng README

name: Grok JPEG 2000 codec
baseline: OpenJPEG (JPEG 2000); also Kakadu (proprietary, via GDAL JP2KAK)
workload: GDAL workflows reading JPEG 2000 imagery: Spot 6 on network storage, Spot 6 on local storage, and a Pleiades region read, using 16 threads and a GDAL release build.
claimed_speedup: README table (Grok JP2Grok vs Kakadu JP2KAK vs OpenJPEG): Spot 6 (Network Storage) 35.17 s vs 344 s vs 85 s; Spot 6 (Local Storage) 26.92 s vs 30.57 s vs 52.09 s; Pleiades (Region) 0.74 s vs 1.41 s vs 4.28 s.
compiler_and_flags: GDAL release build (compiler and flags not stated)
hardware: Fedora 42, 16 threads (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Strong copyleft: AGPL v3 (network use triggers source obligations), a poor fit for permissive-license projects. Adds HTJ2K, random-access sub-image decoding with TLM and PLT markers, a multi-level tile cache and S3 access, which are features of the whole GDAL workflow measured. Reported to have started as an OpenJPEG fork (per third-party descriptions seen in search snippets); GitHub does not mark it as a fork.
caveats: JPEG 2000 is outside the listed baselines (libjpeg-turbo, libpng, libwebp, libavif); OpenJPEG is the widely used open-source incumbent. First-party end-to-end GDAL timings that include I/O, caching and region reads, not codec-only throughput. CPU model, compiler flags and the benchmark inputs are not given in the README.
